pages.text:
What Is Virtualization?
Virtualization creates logical versions of computing resources.
01 / VIRTUALIZATION
Definition
Virtualization creates virtual representations of 
servers, operating systems, storage, or networks.
Physical Resource Abstraction Layer Virtual Resources
07
pages.title: What Is Virtualization?

pages.text:
Before and After Virtualization
Virtualization consolidates multiple workloads onto shared physical infrastructure.
01 / VIRTUALIZATION
Traditional Infrastructure
One physical server is commonly dedicated to one 
major workload.
Virtualized Infrastructure
One physical server can host multiple isolated virtual 
environments.

pages.text:
Physical Machine vs Virtual Machine
A VM behaves like a computer but is defined and managed in software.
01 / VIRTUALIZATION
Physical Machine
• Dedicated hardware
• Usually runs one primary OS
• Hardware-dependent
• Physical maintenance required
• Direct device ownership
Virtual Machine
• Software-defined computer
• Shares physical hardware
• Runs its own guest OS
• Portable as files/images
• Isolated operating environment
09
pages.title: Physical Machine vs Virtual Machine

pages.text:
What Is a Hypervisor?
The hypervisor is the software layer that creates and manages VMs.
02 / HYPERVISORS
Virtual Machine 1 Virtual Machine 2 Virtual Machine 3
HYPERVISOR
PHYSICAL HARDWARE
VMs do not “touch” hardware directly. They interact through the hypervisor.
14
pages.title: What Is a Hypervisor?

pages.text:
Type 1 Hypervisor: Bare-Metal
Runs directly on physical hardware, common in data centers and enterprise virtualization.
02 / HYPERVISORS
VM 1 VM 2 VM 3
Type 1 Hypervisor
Physical Hardware
Examples
Examples include VMware ESXi, Hyper-V Server, Xen, and KVM-based environments. These are examples, not endorsements.
15
pages.title: Type 1 Hypervisor: Bare-Metal

pages.text:
Type 2 Hypervisor: Hosted
Runs as an application on top of a host operating system, common for learning and testing.
02 / HYPERVISORS
VM 1 VM 2
Hypervisor Application
Host Operating System
Physical Hardware
Examples
VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, and Parallels Desktop are common Type 2 examples.

pages.text:
VM Lifecycle
Virtual machines can be created, configured, controlled, saved, and removed as software-defined environments.
02 / VM MANAGEMENT
Create Configure Start Run Snapshot Stop Archive / Delete
VMs are managed objects. They can be copied, paused, restored, and removed more flexibly than physical 
computers.
18

Snapshots and Cloning
Snapshots preserve a VM state; clones create another VM based on an existing one.
02 / VM MANAGEMENT
State A Snapshot Changes Restore

Useful before updates or testing.
Clone
Creates another VM based on an existing 
VM. Useful for repeated environments.

pages.text:
Benefits and Limitations of Virtualization
Virtualization improves flexibility but introduces management and resource trade-offs.
02 / VM MANAGEMENT
Benefits
• Better resource utilization
• Isolation between environments
• Faster deployment
• Easier testing
• Reduced physical infrastructure
• Portability of VM images
Limitations
• Performance overhead
• Resource contention
• Host failure impact
• Licensing concerns
• Management complexity
• Security misconfiguration risk
22
pages.title: Benefits and Limitations of Virtualization

From VM to Cloud
Turning virtualized resources into network-delivered 
services
03 / From VM to Cloud
23
pages.title: From VM to Cloud

pages.text:
Virtualization ≠ Cloud Computing
They are related, but they answer different questions.
03 / VM TO CLOUD
Virtualization
How can computing resources be 
abstracted from physical hardware?
Cloud Computing
How can computing resources be 
delivered as services over a network?
Virtualization can enable cloud infrastructure, but not all virtualization is cloud.
24
pages.title: Virtualization ≠ Cloud Computing

pages.text:
From Server to Cloud
Cloud computing combines virtualization with automation, networking, management, and service delivery.
03 / VM TO CLOUD
Physical
Server
Virtual
Machines
Resource
Pool
Automation &
Management
Network
Access
Cloud
Service
Cloud is not just “someone else’s VM.” It is an operating model for delivering resources on 
demand.
25
pages.title: From Server to Cloud

pages.text:
What Is Cloud Computing?
Computing resources are provided as services over a network.
03 / CLOUD BASICS
Definition
Cloud computing provides resources such as 
compute, storage, platforms, and software 
through network-accessible services.
Plain-language view
Users request services; cloud infrastructure allocates 
and delivers the resources behind the scenes.
26
pages.title: What Is Cloud Computing?

pages.text:
Core Characteristics of Cloud Computing
Cloud computing changes how resources are accessed, allocated, scaled, and measured.
03 / CLOUD BASICS
On-Demand
Request resources when needed
Broad Network Access
Access services over a network
Resource Pooling
Share provider infrastructure
Rapid Elasticity
Scale capacity dynamically
Measured Service
Usage can be monitored and 
billed
27
pages.title: Core Characteristics of Cloud Computing

pages.text:
Scalability vs Elasticity
Scalability expands capacity; elasticity adjusts capacity dynamically as demand changes.
03 / CLOUD BASICS
Scalability
Planned increase or decrease in capacity as 
needs grow.
Example: moving from 2 servers to 10 servers.
Elasticity
Dynamic adjustment of resources in response to 
changing demand.
Example: automatically adding capacity during 
peak usage.
28
pages.title: Scalability vs Elasticity

pages.title: Deployment & Practice

pages.text:
Cloud Deployment Models
Deployment models describe where cloud resources live and how they are shared or connected.
05 / DEPLOYMENT
Public Cloud
Shared provider infrastructure.
Private Cloud
Dedicated cloud environment for one organization.
Hybrid Cloud
Connected private and public environments.
Multi-Cloud
Use services from multiple cloud providers.
37
pages.title: Cloud Deployment Models

pages.text:
Hybrid Cloud vs Multi-Cloud
Hybrid and multi-cloud are related but not identical concepts.
05 / DEPLOYMENT
Hybrid Cloud
Different infrastructure environments connected 
together.
Example: private infrastructure connected to 
public cloud resources.
Multi-Cloud
Use of services from multiple cloud providers.
Example: provider A for compute, provider B for 
analytics, provider C for backup.
38
pages.title: Hybrid Cloud vs Multi-Cloud

pages.text:
Why Use Cloud Computing?
Cloud can increase flexibility, speed, access, and resilience when managed well.
05 / VALUE
CLOUD V ALUE
Rapid deployment
 Flexible capacity
 Global access
 Managed services
Backup / recovery
 Collaboration
 Automation
 Scalability
Cloud is valuable when the service model matches the workload and the organization manages cost, security, and governance.
39
pages.title: Why Use Cloud Computing?

pages.text:
Cloud Risks and Challenges
Cloud computing changes operational risks rather than eliminating them.
05 / RISKS
Security
 Privacy
 Compliance
 Outages
Internet dependency
 Vendor dependency
 Uncontrolled cost
 Configuration errors
A good cloud design includes governance, monitoring, security configuration, and cost control.
40
pages.title: Cloud Risks and Challenges

pages.text:
Shared Responsibility for Security
Cloud provider and customer responsibilities differ by service model.
05 / SECURITY
Cloud Provider
Security OF the Cloud
• Physical data center
• Core infrastructure
• Underlying platform
• Global service availability mechanisms
Customer
Security IN the Cloud
• User accounts
• Permissions
• Configurations
• Application data
• Access policies
Exact responsibility depends on IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS.
41
pages.title: Shared Responsibility for Security

Containers virtualize at the operating-system level; VMs virtualize hardware environments.

Stronger environment isolation, heavier footprint.

pages.text:
Classification Activity
Classify each scenario as VM, IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS.
05 / ACTIVITY
Scenario 1
Run Linux inside your Windows 
laptop.
Scenario 2
Rent a virtual server online.
Scenario 3
Deploy code without managing 
the OS.
Scenario 4
Use an online email application.
Scenario 5
Test software in an isolated OS.
Scenario 6
Use a cloud-based learning 
platform.
Students answer first, then discuss why responsibility and delivery model matter.
44
pages.title: Classification Activity

pages.text:
Scenario Answer Why
1. Run Linux inside your Windows 
laptop. VM
Linux runs as a guest operating 
system inside a virtual machine on 
the Windows host.
2. Rent a virtual server online. IaaS
The cloud provider supplies 
virtualized compute infrastructure, 
while you typically manage the OS 
and applications.
3. Deploy code without managing 
the OS. PaaS
You focus on application code 
while the provider manages the 
OS, runtime, and underlying 
infrastructure.
4. Use an online email application. SaaS
You use a complete software 
application delivered over the 
Internet without managing its 
infrastructure.
5. Test software in an isolated OS. VM
A VM provides an isolated 
operating-system environment for 
testing.
6. Use a cloud-based learning 
platform. SaaS
Students and instructors use a 
complete application delivered 
through the cloud.
pages.title: Scenario Answer Why

pages.text:
06 / WRAP-UP
From Hardware to Cloud Services
Key takeaway: virtualization abstracts resources; cloud computing delivers resources as services.
Physical Hardware Operating System Hypervisor Virtual Machines Resource Pool Cloud Services
Takeaway 1
Virtualization abstracts physical resources.
Takeaway 2
A VM behaves like an independent computer.
Takeaway 3
IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS differ by management 
responsibility.
Exit question: If virtual machines already exist, why do we need cloud computing?
45
